To solve this problem, we need to consider the permutation graph. The permutation graph is a directed graph with $n$ vertices, where each vertex $i$ has one outgoing edge to vertex $p_i$.

Since each vertex has exactly one outgoing edge and exactly one incoming edge, the graph decomposes into cycles. To sort a permutation by swapping elements, it is enough to sort each cycle separately: let the vertices of a cycle be $v_1, v_2, \dots, v_k$ in order; we can swap $p_{v_1}$ with $p_{v_2}$, then $p_{v_1}$ with $p_{v_3}$, and so on.

This means that, in this problem, if all vertices within each cycle of the permutation have the same color, the permutation can be sorted. On the other hand, if at least one cycle contains two vertices of different colors, it contains two adjacent vertices of different colors, and the number at one of them cannot be moved to the other.

Therefore, Bob's goal is to make some cycle contain vertices of both colors, while Alice's goal is to prevent this.

In the rest of the editorial, we assume that $k \ge 2$; the case $k = 1$ must be solved separately (it depends on the length of the longest cycle and the parity of $n$).

Consider the cycle lengths. If the permutation contains a cycle of length at least $k+2$, Bob always wins: if Alice is the first to color a vertex in this cycle, Bob can paint another vertex in the opposite color. If Alice does not make a move in this cycle, Bob can color one vertex of the cycle red. After Alice's next turn, at least one uncolored vertex will remain in that same cycle, and Bob can color it blue.

Now only cycles of length $k+1$ or less remain. If there are at least two cycles of length $k+1$, Bob wins: if Alice does not make moves in these cycles, Bob can color one vertex in each of them red. After Alice's next turn, at least one of these cycles will still contain an uncolored vertex, which Bob can color blue.

There are two cases left: either there is one cycle of length $k+1$, or there are none. If there is exactly one cycle of length $k+1$, Alice must color all cycles of lengths from $2$ to $k$ on her first turn: if at least one of them remains, Bob colors one vertex in the cycle of length $k+1$ and one vertex in the remaining cycle, and Alice cannot color all the uncolored vertices in that cycle on her turn. Let the total length of such cycles be $l$.

If Alice colors all such cycles, only cycles of length $1$ and the cycle of length $k+1$ remain after her turn. Alice's goal is to force Bob to be the first to make a move in this cycle (otherwise, she loses). If the number of cycles of length $1$ at the start of Bob's turn is divisible by $(k+1)$, Alice wins: she has a symmetric strategy (if Bob does not color the large cycle but colors $b$ cycles of length $1$, Alice can color $k+1-b$ cycles of length $1$, making the number of cycles of length $1$ divisible by $(k+1)$ again). If this number is not divisible by $(k+1)$ at the start of Bob's turn, Bob can use the same symmetric strategy against Alice and force her to make a move in the large cycle first. Therefore, if the number of cycles of length $1$ modulo $(k+1)$ is $c$, Alice must color exactly $c$ such cycles.

If $l + c = 0$ or $l + c  \gt  k$, Alice cannot make a suitable move and loses. Otherwise, she wins using the symmetric strategy described above.

The remaining case is when all cycles have length $k$ or less. In this case, Alice can color entire cycles, and Bob can win only if, at the start of his turn, there is a set of $d \le k$ cycles containing at least $d + k + 1$ vertices in total: he can color one vertex in each of these cycles, and after Alice's next turn, at least one of them will still contain an uncolored vertex. If there is no such set of cycles, Alice can respond to every move by Bob that leaves some cycles partially colored.

Alice's goal is now to make her first move so that no such set of cycles remains. How can we check whether this is possible? Sort the cycles in descending order of length and keep only the $2k$ longest ones (the others are not worth considering for Bob). Then use dynamic programming: $dp_{i,j,x}$ means that we have considered the first $i$ cycles, and Alice has colored $j$ of them, with a total length of $x$. The value of the state is the minimum possible sum of $(l-1)$ over the largest cycles that Bob will take.

The transitions are as follows: either Alice colors the next cycle herself (moving to $dp_{i+1, j+1, x+l}$, where $l$ is the length of the next cycle), or she leaves it to Bob (moving to $dp_{i+1, j, x}$ and adding $l-1$ to the value if Bob can take one more cycle, that is, if $i - j  \lt  k$). If there exists a state $dp_{m,j,x} \le k$ (where $m$ is the number of cycles), Alice can choose which cycles to color on her first turn; otherwise, she loses.

This dynamic programming is the most complex part of the solution, and it runs in $O(\min(n, k) \cdot k^2)$, so the solution comfortably fits within the time limit.

Choose a threshold $B = O(\log^2 V)$ with $B \gt \max f(i)$. For any $n \in [2^k, 2^{k + 1} - B]$, the second option costs $2^{k + 1} - n + k \gt f(n)$, so it is never optimal, and therefore $f(n) = f(n - 2^k + 2) + k + 1$. In other words, the second option only matters for the last fewer than $B$ values of each interval $[2^k, 2^{k + 1})$.

Using this, we can compute $g(n)$ piece by piece. Let $2^k \le n \lt 2^{k + 1}$ and $w = \max(2^k - 1, \min(n, 2^{k + 1} - B))$ (the outer $\max$ only matters for small $k$, where the whole interval lies beyond the threshold). Then
 $ \begin{aligned} g(n) &= g(2^k - 1) + \sum \limits_{i = 2^k}^w f(i) + \sum \limits_{i = w + 1}^n f(i)\\ &= g(2^k - 1) + \sum \limits_{i = 2^k}^w (f(i - 2^k + 2) + k + 1) + \sum \limits_{i = w + 1}^n f(i)\\ &= g(2^k - 1) + \sum \limits_{i = 2}^{w - 2^k + 2} (f(i) + k + 1) + \sum \limits_{i = w + 1}^n f(i)\\ &= g(2^k - 1) + g(w - 2^k + 2) - g(1) + (w - 2^k + 1)(k + 1) + \sum \limits_{i = w + 1}^n f(i). \end{aligned} $
For the last term, note that $n - w = O(\log^2 V)$. So for each $k$ we precompute $f$ and its prefix sums at all positions in $(2^{k + 1} - B, 2^{k + 1})$. This is $O(\log^3 V)$ values of $f$ in total, each computed in $O(\log V)$, so this part takes $O(\log^4 V)$ time.

The values $g(2^k - 1)$ and $g(2^k - B + 2)$ only depend on smaller values of the same two forms, so we can precompute all of them in increasing order of $k$.

Now for a query $g(n)$, apply the formula above. If $w = 2^{k + 1} - B$, then $g(w - 2^k + 2) = g(2^k - B + 2)$ is already precomputed and we are done. Otherwise, $w = n$, and we recurse into $g(n - 2^k + 2)$, where $n - 2^k + 2 \lt 2^k$, so the highest bit strictly decreases. Hence the recursion depth is $O(\log V)$, and each query takes $O(\log V)$ time.

Time complexity: $O(\log^4 V + t \log V)$.

Bonus

The threshold can be made exact. Appending one type-2 operation shows $f(n) \le f(n + 1) + 1$, so $h(n) = f(n) + n$ is non-decreasing. With $m = n - 2^k + 2$, the first option of the recursion is optimal if and only if $f(m) + k + 1 \le 2^{k + 1} - n + k$, that is, $h(m) \le 2^k + 1$. Hence the valid values of $m$ form a prefix; let $\mathrm{pos}_k$ be its last element. Then $f(n) = f(n - 2^k + 2) + k + 1$ for $n \in [2^k, \mathrm{pos}_k + 2^k - 2]$, and $f(n) = 2^{k + 1} - n + k$ for the rest of the interval. Since the valid values form a prefix, $\mathrm{pos}_k$ can be found by binary search, which takes $O(\log^3 V)$ in total.

The rest is the same as before, except that the part beyond the threshold is now an arithmetic progression and can be summed in $O(1)$. Let $w = \min(n, \mathrm{pos}_k + 2^k - 2)$. Then
 $ g(n) = g(2^k - 1) + g(w - 2^k + 2) - g(1) + (w - 2^k + 1)(k + 1) + \frac{1}{2}(2^{k + 2} + 2k - w - n - 1)(n - w). $
We precompute $g(2^k - 1)$ in increasing order of $k$ as before. The term $g(w - 2^k + 2)$ does not even need precomputation. Since $f(m) \ge 2$ for $m \ge 2$, we have $h(m) \ge m + 2$, so $\mathrm{pos}_k \le 2^k - 1$ and thus $w - 2^k + 2 \lt 2^k$. Hence we can compute it recursively: each call makes only one recursive call and the highest bit strictly decreases, so the recursion depth is $O(\log V)$.

Time complexity: $O(\log^3 V + t \log V)$.

Computing $\mathrm{pos}_k$ in $O(\log V)$

Recall that $\mathrm{pos}_k$ is the largest $m$ with $h(m) = f(m) + m \le 2^k + 1$. Let a type-1 operation that adds $2^j$ cost $2^j + 1$, and let a type-2 operation be free. Every step then costs $1$ plus the change of $x$, so the minimum cost to reach $n$ is exactly $h(n)$, and $\mathrm{pos}_k$ is the largest $x$ reachable with budget $2^k + 1$.

A maximal block of $i$ type-1 operations adds $2^i - 1$ and costs $2^i + i - 1$. In an optimal solution, all blocks have distinct lengths: two blocks of length $j \ge 2$ can be merged into one block of length $j + 1$, which gives a larger $x$ at no extra cost, and a block of length $1$ other than the first one only cancels the type-2 operation before it. Now let $i$ be the largest length that fits into the budget. If every block were shorter than $i$, we would get $x \le \sum_{j = 1}^{i - 1} (2^j - 1) \lt 2^i - 1$, which is worse than a single block of length $i$. So the longest block has length exactly $i$, and we repeat the argument with the remaining budget.

Therefore, we go through $i = k, k - 1, \ldots, 2$ and take a block of length $i$ whenever its cost $2^i + i - 1$ fits into the remaining budget. The first block adds $2^i - 1$, and every later one, together with the type-2 operation before it, adds $2^i - 2$, so $\mathrm{pos}_k = 1 + \sum (2^i - 2)$ over the chosen $i$. This takes $O(\log V)$ for each $k$, so the precomputation now takes only $O(\log^2 V)$ time.

Time complexity: $O(\log^2 V + t \log V)$.

Consider a single R in $s$ at position $i$. There are two cases.

Case 1: there is a W in front of this R. Let $j$ be the index of the nearest such W. It is not hard to see that, by inserting $t$, we can make the answer take every value in $[j, j+m]$, where $m = |t|$. Clearly the answer can never be smaller than $i$, but it can be larger. Now look at the last occurrence of W in $t$ (say it is the $k$-th character of $t$): we may read it last, and then the answer can also reach $i-1+k$. This part is contiguous as well, so the set of attainable answers is exactly the interval $[j, \max(j+m, i-1+k)]$.

Case 2: there is no W in front of this R. Then $0$ is attainable, and we can compute the answer directly. Take a W of $t$ at position $j$; it lets $[j, j+i-1]$ be absorbed into the answer interval. Hence the answer is the size of the union of all intervals $[j, j+i-1]$.

To get the answer for every R, iterate over $i$ from left to right; then all these intervals grow simultaneously. We maintain the number of currently alive intervals, and for each of them the moment at which it catches up with the next interval; at those moments we subtract its contribution and retire it.

Complexity: $O(n+m)$.

editorial.tutorial:
Note what happens to the robot's diagonal $d = r + c$. Moving up or right adds $1$, moving down-left subtracts $2$. Since $-2 \equiv +1 \pmod{3}$, the value of $d$ goes up by $1$ modulo $3$ every second, regardless of the robot's move. If the robot starts on diagonal $d_0$, then at second $s$ it is on a diagonal $d_s$ with $$d_s \equiv d_0 + s - 1 \pmod{3}.$$ In other words, the starting square determines the value of $d \pmod{3}$ at all times.

With this in mind, the following construction works. The shots are split into three blocks of consecutive seconds, one for each value of $d_0 \pmod{3}$. In the block for residue $\rho$, starting at second $s$, those robots are on $d \equiv \rho + s - 1 \pmod{3}$. We use as the first shot the largest diagonal $V \le 2n$ of that class, and every following second the shot drops by $2$, $$v = V,\; V-2,\; V-4,\; \dots$$ down to the smallest one $\ge 2$. Every shot lands in the same class as the robot, since dropping by $2$ per second is the same as going up by $1$ modulo $3$, which is exactly the speed at which the group's residue advances.

It remains to show that each block catches its whole group. Take a robot with $d_0 \equiv \rho \pmod{3}$ and let $g = d - v$ be the difference between its diagonal and the shot. Since $d$ and $v$ are always in the same class modulo $3$, $g$ is always a multiple of $3$. It also never decreases. If the robot moves up or right, $d$ goes up $1$ and $v$ drops $2$, so $g$ grows by $3$. If it moves down-left both drop by $2$ and $g$ stays the same. In other words, once the laser is above the robot, the robot can never end up above it again.

At the start $v = V$ is the largest diagonal of the class, so $g \le 0$. At the end $v$ is the smallest one, so $g \ge 0$. Since $g$ goes from $\le 0$ to $\ge 0$ without ever decreasing and only in multiples of $3$, at some second it must equal exactly $0$, meaning the laser lands on the robot's diagonal.

Each block uses at most $n$ shots, so $3n$ lasers always suffice.

Implement a function $get(i, k)$ that, for each $i$, can find the $k$-th smallest $a_i\oplus a_j$ among all $j$ (not necessarily greater than $i$). Create an array $cnt$ of length $n$, where initially $cnt_i = 0$ for each $1\le i\le n$. Now for the transformations:

 Maintain $get(i, cnt_i)$ in increasing order.

 Choose the minimum among them and add it to a vector. After adding it, increase $cnt_i$ by $1$.

 Since $a_i\oplus a_j$ is added twice, perform exactly $2n$ additions. After that, replace the array $a$ with the elements of the vector at odd positions.

Thus, the transformations take $O(n\log(A))$ time. The total complexity is $O(n \log^2(A))$ time and $O(n\log(A))$ memory.
